latest.title: From the best and worst companies to how to get treated fairly - ask our consumer champion anything – live
latest.summary: In her weekly column for the Guardian, Anna Tims solves readers consumer problems – ranging from the devastating to the ridiculous . She’s online now to answer your questions and share her wisdom Sign in or sign up to post your question Janubian asks : How do you manage the emotions that letter writers’ situations must trigger - for example frustration, anger and sadness at the inhumanity of so many companies and their employees to those they are meant to serve? Anna: That’s an interesting question. When I started writing consumer columns, I was fighting the good fight over faulty kettles or disappointing holidays. Over the last few years, it’s felt sometimes more like social work. It’s hard to maintain professional detachment when a nonagenarian is suffering in a decaying council flat or an energy company is stonewalling someone with terminal cancer. The cases that haunt me at night are those who have just lost a child or a partner and are being tormented by a merciless multi-national. And there are cases that remain with me for years afterwards. It can be difficult not to let professional obligation tip over into personal investment. It would be inappropriate to keep in personal touch with those readers. But sometimes it’s hard not knowing how they are getting on. Anna: Check if the company has published a complaints procedure on its website, then follow it. It should tell you the various stages of escalation if you’re not getting anywhere. Keep a timeline of interactions with the company, including the date and substance of phone calls. If you complain via webchat download a transcript to take screenshots and copy any letter you post. It’s important to have a paper trail to prove your efforts to resolve the problem. Companies dislike a public shaming so a complaint on Twitter or Bluesky can sometimes galvanise inert corporate conscience. Take it to the top if need be. The website ceoemail.com publishes contact details of CEOs. If the firm is part of an ombudsman or alternative dispute resolution scheme, that is your next step once you’ve exhausted all other avenues. Then the small claims court is the last resort. Continue reading...

Business.title: Oil falls below $100 a barrel on reports Iran ‘makes strait of Hormuz offer’; UK government borrowing paints ‘dismal picture’ – business live
Business.summary: The rising cost of servicing the UK national debt pushed up borrowing last month, while oil is dropping, and M&G holds Bond Vigilantes Forum in London How much ‘headroom’ might John Healey still have to keep within the government’s fiscal rules? That’s the question dogging Westminster and the City. “The chancellor has probably lost about half the headroom he inherited, leaving it between £10bn to £15bn. As long as the headroom is in double figures, he will probably be able to avoid topping it up, but the drop in headroom means any additional day-to-day spending, such as on defence or cost of living, will have to be paid for by higher taxes. “What’s more, if the recent rise in energy prices is sustained through the next few months, household energy bills could rise by another 25% in January, which would take them above the level that the previous government capped them at. That would only further increase the pressure to act on cost of living by temporarily subsiding energy bills. “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them. Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts. Everyone can diagnose the problem, but it’s far from clear that a PM who swept to power promising good things for all is capable of holding a fractious Labour party together to carry out the tough work needed.” Continue reading...

Science.title: This emerging treatment could help people avoid knee replacement surgery
Science.summary: A minimally invasive procedure called genicular artery embolization could offer a new middle ground between conservative treatments and knee replacement for osteoarthritis. By blocking tiny blood vessels associated with inflammation, GAE can significantly reduce pain, with some patients reporting little or no pain afterward. Studies suggest the benefits may last two to four years in people who respond well.

Science.title: For the first time, scientists watch sound jump between quantum states
Science.summary: Stanford researchers have recorded the first real-time quantum jumps of sound, watching single phonons abruptly vanish from one energy state to another. The breakthrough could open new paths for quantum computing, error correction, highly sensitive biological sensors, and next-generation sound-based devices.

Science.title: Humpback whale mother may have mourned her dead calf for days
Science.summary: Researchers observed a humpback whale mother staying beside her presumed stillborn calf for hours and possibly days off Australia’s Gold Coast. She maintained eye contact and remained close to the calf in behavior resembling caregiving and nurturing. Scientists say the rare observation may provide new insight into grief, maternal attachment, and emotional complexity in humpback whales.

Science.title: This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
Science.summary: Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.

Culture.title: Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists review – It caused fury across Europe. In the UK? Laughter and coughing
Culture.summary: National Theatre, London Tiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing What does it say about an audience who, while watching a character make a speech that has sparked screeching protests and angry walkouts in its run across Europe, sit politely listening until the end? The booing does come, but only after the actor playing a far-right politician and kidnap victim (Romeu Costa) has finished a half-hour invective that takes in everything from the scourge of minorities to that of elites, homosexuals, and the far-left. It is a masterclass in rightwing rabble-rousing, with its appropriation of the word “freedom”. Yet on press night at its British premiere, all that is summoned in response is nervous laughter, a chorus of coughs and a few loud whistles. Continue reading...

Culture.title: The amazing life of 101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser: ‘We made noise. We closed the streets’
Culture.summary: Sick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a day In January of 1971, the American art historian Linda Nochlin published a landmark essay, Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists? It was a provocation and a call to arms that was to send shockwaves through the arts establishment. “It wasn’t just a problem for artists,” says Ce Roser, more than half a century on. “My older friends could not get shows, although they had had brilliant careers before, and that happened also to all of my friends who were poets or writers. Nobody seemed to be able to establish themselves as career artists. So we got together, we complained, and I decided we should have a meeting and really talk seriously about it.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: Post your questions for Miranda Richardson
Culture.summary: She has lit up screens large and small playing Ruth Ellis, Rita Skeeter, Barbara Castle and the hilarious Queenie in Blackadder. Alternatively, you could ask about birds of prey, orangutans or playing the cello Judging by the size of her awards cupboard, Miranda Richardson has had quite the career. She won a Bafta for the 1992 psychological drama Damage, opposite Jeremy Irons, and Golden Globes for the 1991 historical drama Enchanted April and the 1994 Nazi thriller Fatherland, and was Oscar-nominated for both Damage and the 1994 historical drama Tom & Viv. Her other notable performances include IRA member Jude in The Crying Game, Ruth Ellis in Dance With a Stranger and Lady Van Tassel in Sleepy Hollow. She’s pretty handy at comedy, too – and probably just as familiar for playing acid-tongued Daily Prophet journalist Rita Skeeter in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, the murderous chicken-farm owner Mrs Tweedy in Chicken Run and, of course, the gloriously unhinged Queenie in Blackadder II: “I may have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a concrete elephant.” Continue reading...
